definition: The essay's interpretive grid, set out in the prologue. Critiques of religion do not form a continuous tradition: they belong to eight distinct regimes, which do not aim at the same thing. Religion appears in turn as an error to be corrected (Epicurus, Lucretius, Spinoza, Hume, d'Holbach, Feuerbach), a symptom of a world that needs it (Marx), a value whose genealogy is traced (Nietzsche), a component of metaphysics, onto-theology (Heidegger), an illusion commanded by desire (Freud), a social function (Durkheim, Weber), an inheritance whose secularization is disputed (Schmitt, Löwith, Blumenberg, Gauchet, Taylor, Habermas), or an experience that survives dogmas (Schleiermacher, James, Otto, Bergson, Bataille). Ricoeur groups the second, third and fifth under the name of the school of suspicion. The eighth regime obliges the essay to widen religion to include spirituality. These regimes do not add up, they accuse one another: each reproaches the previous one with having remained religious, which the essay calls the law of refoundations.

The criterion the essay proposes for deciding whether an exit from religion has refounded another. In its final formulation (conclusion), one refounds a religion, in the sense that matters, not when one occupies a place that theology has left empty, but when one installs in that place an absolute in whose name the sacrifice of the individual can be demanded, and criticism of which becomes sacrilege; freely consented self-offering does not fall under it. The criterion does not depend on the presence or absence of God: believers have left religion in the sense in which Barth, Bonhoeffer and Weil denounce it, and atheists have remained in it. It distinguishes two degrees: strict refoundation, where the absolute demands (Plato, Rousseau, Comte, the secular religions, Schmitt), and soft refoundation, where one consecrates without demanding (Feuerbach, Ferry). The essay owes it more to Stirner, for whom the fear of Man is a modified form of the fear of God, than to Löwith; Girard gives it an anthropological foundation, since to refound is to designate a victim. See also secular religions, the sacred.

The two ancient etymologies of the word religion, which the essay turns into two conceptions of the thing. For Cicero (*De natura deorum* II, 72), *religio* comes from *relegere*, to read again, to go over scrupulously: religion is ritual and civic exactness, the correct observance of what concerns the worship of the gods, with neither dogma nor inner faith. For Lactantius (*Divine Institutes* IV, 28), tutor to Constantine's son, it comes from *religare*, to bind: the bond of piety that ties man to God, and which presupposes a personal relation. The second, Christian etymology won out in usage; modern linguists consider the first the more probable. The essay reads in them the opposition that runs through the sciences of religion: Durkheim, for whom religion is a collective fact with a Church, stands on Cicero's side; William James, for whom it is the experience of individuals in their solitude, on the side of the solitary mystic. See also spirituality, the sacred.

In the sense the essay adopts, that of Foucault and Hadot: the search, the practice and the experience through which the subject carries out on itself the transformations necessary to gain access to the truth (*The Hermeneutics of the Subject*, lecture of 6 January 1982). Hadot speaks of spiritual exercises. The notion presupposes neither God, nor worship, nor belief, which makes it possible to speak of spiritualities without God. The essay draws from it the distinction that runs through it: religion in the strong sense involves an external absolute to which the individual is subjected, dogmas and a community; spirituality involves only an exercise through which the subject transforms itself. There is religion without spirituality, the observance Kant calls *Afterdienst*, and spirituality without God, among the Epicureans, in Spinoza or in Comte-Sponville. It is the eighth regime of critique, the regime of experience, that obliges the essay to widen religion in this way. The essay's answer to its question takes the form of a spirituality of exercise, of which Spinoza gives the ontology, Hadot the historical description and Wittgenstein the strictest limit. See also spiritual exercises.

A word of Kant's, which Heidegger takes up to name the constitution of Western metaphysics since Plato and Aristotle. Metaphysics asks a double question, that of beings as beings (ontology) and that of the supreme being which grounds all the rest (theology); the two merge in a God who is cause of himself, *causa sui*. Heidegger concludes, in *Identität und Differenz* (1957), that this god of the philosophers has nothing divine about it: before the *causa sui*, man can neither pray nor sacrifice, neither fall on his knees nor make music and dance, and godless thinking is perhaps closer to the divine god. Its ancient source is Aristotle's theological philosophy (*Metaphysics* E 1). The essay makes it the fourth regime of critique: the death of God as the common completion of metaphysics and Christianity, foreseen by Pascal, who sets the God of Abraham against that of the philosophers, and turned around by Marion, for whom the god of onto-theology is a conceptual idol. It retains from Heidegger that the critique of the God of the philosophers is not the critique of God. See also idol and icon, negative theology.

langue: also apophatic, from Greek ἀπόφασις (apophasis), negation
definition: A way of speaking of God by denying of him everything that can be said, because every positive attribute would lower him to the rank of creatures. It is also called apophatic, from the Greek *apophasis*, negation. It runs through Plotinus, for whom the One is beyond thought and being, Pseudo-Dionysius, Maimonides, whose *Guide for the Perplexed* (I, 58-59) holds that we know of God only negative attributes and that for him silence is praise, and Meister Eckhart, who prays God to rid him of God. The essay sees in it the anticipation of the regime of experience, and the site of a constructed confrontation: Feuerbach takes negative theology for a subtle and cunning atheism, which keeps the name of God after emptying it of its content; the essay judges that Feuerbach is right about the ordinary believer and Maimonides about the philosopher. Spinoza, in the *Theological-Political Treatise* (VII), judges Maimonides' method useless, dangerous and absurd (attested response). Plotinus, Maimonides and Eckhart appear in the conclusion among the precursors of the exceptions. See also onto-theology.

In Greek, word and reason: the divine reason or word by which the world is ordered. The Stoics make it the immanent reason of the world. In Philo of Alexandria, who reads Genesis with the *Timaeus*, the Logos is the intelligible world, intermediary between God and the world, and at times a second God. The prologue of John (1, 1 and 1, 14) makes it the Word with God, then the Word made flesh. In Justin, the Logos is sown in every man (*logos spermatikos*), which allows Socrates to be called a Christian before Christ, at once an opening towards philosophy and an annexation of it. Augustine finds among the Platonists the Logos with God, but not the Incarnation. In Part Two the essay follows this passage by which the God of the Greek philosophers enters Christianity: the transformation of a crucified prophet into the incarnate Logos matters more to it than the question of Jesus' existence. Freud, in 1927, would call science “our god Logos”. See also onto-theology.

A doctrine attributed to the Latin Averroists of the thirteenth century: a proposition could be true in philosophy and false in theology, or the reverse. Averroes never taught it; the *Decisive Treatise* (*Faṣl al-maqāl*) holds on the contrary that truth cannot be contrary to truth, that there is only one truth and two modes of access to it, the apparent meaning for the people and interpretation (*taʾwīl*) for the men of demonstration. The expression comes from the condemnation pronounced in Paris in 1277 by Bishop Étienne Tempier, who in his prologue reproaches masters of the faculty of arts with saying things true according to philosophy and false according to faith, and from its polemical readers. The essay takes the double truth for a legend, but retains from Averroes a real solution, the sharing of truth between an elite and a multitude, which it judges the most stable of all and finds again in Spinoza, Comte, Renan and Leo Strauss: Averroes does not leave religion and founds nothing, he divides.

A position that grounds religion on faith alone by ruining reason's claims to know God. The word is modern; the thing goes back to the Christian scepticism of the Renaissance. In Montaigne, the *Apology for Raymond Sebond* (*Essays* II, 12) humbles human reason, unable to make a mite and yet making gods by the dozen, and leaves received faith intact: one is a Christian as one is a man of Périgord or a German, by custom. The essay holds this fideism to be sincere, not the mask of an atheist, but notes its uncontrolled effect: if reason can do nothing, custom remains the only explanation of religion, and Montaigne announces Hume. Pascal answers him in an attested response (*Conversation with M. de Sacy*, fragments 62-64), and Bayle and, in another key, Kierkegaard inherit it. Montaigne enters into no refoundation; his motto is a question, and he remains within a tradition.

langue: Greek θεός (theos), god, and δίκη (dikê), justice
definition: A word coined by Leibniz (*Theodicy: Essays on the Goodness of God, the Freedom of Man and the Origin of Evil*, Amsterdam, 1710) for the justification of God in the face of the existence of evil. God, who chose among all possible worlds, created the best; the metaphysical, physical and moral evil of the part serves the perfection of the whole. The book answers Pierre Bayle, who had died four years earlier (attested response). Voltaire mocks it in *Candide* (1759), and Ivan Karamazov gives, for the essay, the moral answer to it: he refuses the final harmony if it costs a child's tear, and returns his ticket. The essay judges that theodicy accepts the sacrifice of the individual to harmony and asks each person to sacrifice their complaint. In the broad sense, the word designates any attempt to give meaning to suffering; Berger notes that what theodicy provides is not first of all happiness, but meaning. See also opium of the people.

Belief in a creator God, architect of the universe and guarantor of morality, established by reason alone, without revelation, dogmas or Churches. The word appears in the sixteenth century and designates in the eighteenth the natural religion of the English and French Enlightenment. It is the position of Voltaire, who fights *l'Infâme*, superstition, fanaticism and the Church, but keeps a Supreme Being as the foundation of morality and a social restraint: if he did not exist, he would have to be invented, and let the sage proclaim him and kings fear him. D'Holbach holds deism to be a half-measure, and Voltaire answers him (*Dieu, dieux*, 1771). Hume ruins its proofs in the *Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion*. The essay classes Voltaire among the transfers of the sacred: he invents a useful God, and Ivan Karamazov quotes his line as the very programme of the Grand Inquisitor. Kant, later, keeps God as a postulate of practical reason, which is another way of keeping what is reasonable.

In Rousseau (*The Social Contract* IV, 8, 1762), a purely civil profession of faith, whose articles the sovereign fixes not as dogmas of religion but as sentiments of sociability: the existence of a powerful and beneficent divinity, the life to come, the happiness of the just and the punishment of the wicked, the sanctity of the social contract and the laws, and a single negative dogma, the exclusion of intolerance. Whoever does not believe it may be banished, not as impious but as unsociable; whoever, having acknowledged it, behaves as if not believing it must be punished with death. Rousseau distinguishes it from the religion of man (the Gospel, too detached from the city) and from the religion of the priest (Catholicism, which divides sovereignty). The essay knows of no text that illustrates its criterion more exactly: Rousseau leaves the Church through the heart, with the *Profession of Faith of the Savoyard Vicar*, and re-enters religion through the city. Robespierre and the cult of the Supreme Being (1794) did not betray this chapter. Strict refoundation; Plato (*Laws* X) is its original, by constructed confrontation.

In Schleiermacher (*Der christliche Glaube*, 1821-1822), the essence of piety: the consciousness of being absolutely dependent, that is, of being in relation with God. The *Glaubenslehre* systematizes what the *Speeches on Religion* of 1799 said in other words: religion is neither knowledge nor morality, but intuition and feeling, sense and taste for the infinite. Hegel mocks the formula in his preface to Hinrichs (1822): if religion were the feeling of dependence, the dog would be the best Christian (attested response). Feuerbach takes it up and turns it around in his Heidelberg lectures (1851): man depends first of all on nature, and it is nature that religion deifies (attested response). Otto, in 1917, corrects it with the creature-feeling, which presupposes the inaccessibility of its object. The essay sees in it the structural weakness of every regime of experience: experience proves that one feels, it does not prove what one feels. See also numinous.

The dialectical movement in Hegel, for which French has no word: *aufheben* means at once to abolish, to preserve and to raise up. Applied to religion, *Aufhebung* means that philosophy surpasses religious representation by preserving it in the concept: religion is not refuted, it is comprehended. For Hegel, religion and philosophy have the same content, absolute Spirit; religion thinks it in the form of representation (images, narratives, the Father and the Son), philosophy in the form of the concept. The death of God, in *Glauben und Wissen* (1802), is a speculative Good Friday followed by a resurrection; Nietzsche will keep the death without the resurrection. The essay judges the argument right and the conclusion wrong: philosophy becomes the higher religion of the wise, and the Averroist division between the elite and the people returns. Kierkegaard answers him that subjectivity is truth (attested response); Barth takes up the word to say that revelation abolishes and fulfils religion. See also death of God.

Feuerbach's thesis (*Das Wesen des Christentums*, 1841): man places outside himself, in a God, the qualities of his own species (*Gattung*), reason, will, love, and then kneels before them. The secret of theology is anthropology, and the consciousness of God is the self-consciousness of man. The word projection comes from the vocabulary of his readers; Feuerbach speaks of objectification and alienation. D'Holbach and Lucretius had foreseen it, Durkheim will transpose it to the group, Freud will connect it to desire. It is the heart of the first regime of critique, the regime of error, in its most accomplished form. Stirner answers in 1844 that predicates transferred to man do not lose their divinity: Feuerbach's Man is a new God; Marx, in the sixth thesis (1845), that the human essence is the ensemble of social relations; Barth, in 1927, grants that he is right all along the line about religion as human experience. The essay takes Feuerbach as the textbook case of soft refoundation: he abandons the name of God but keeps the thing, adoration. See also illusion.

Marx's formula in the *Introduction to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right* (1844), usually quoted without the sentence that precedes it: religion is the sigh of the oppressed creature, the heart of a heartless world, the spirit of a spiritless situation, and, just before, the protest against real distress. Nineteenth-century opium is a painkiller, not a pleasure drug: religion soothes a pain it did not cause. It is a symptom, and one does not abolish the symptom without changing the world that produces it; to demand that people give up illusions is to demand that they give up a condition that needs illusions. This is the second regime of critique. The essay retains above all the Protest: the wisdoms of immanence, Spinoza before Ivan, Comte-Sponville before Hausemer, console without protesting, and consolation becomes in the conclusion the indicator of a refoundation; Simone Weil, a believer, removes the opium without removing the protest. Marx dismissed the sacred; he did not dismiss salvation. See also theodicy.

The poem Ivan recites to his brother Alyosha in *The Brothers Karamazov* (1879-1880, Book V, chapter 5). Christ returns to Seville at the time of the Inquisition; an old cardinal has him arrested and reproaches him for having refused, in the three temptations in the desert, miracle, mystery and authority, and for having left men a freedom they cannot bear. The Church has corrected his work: it gives bread and governs consciences, at the price of the lie of a few who no longer believe. Christ answers nothing and kisses him: a gesture, not an argument. The essay makes it the touchstone of its whole question, the figure of the one who leaves God while keeping religion, and the political completion of Feuerbach, a Comte become lucid, and therefore tragic. Plato is its ancestor (*Laws* X), Voltaire wrote its programme, Demopheles in Schopenhauer is the version without tragedy, Onfray the contemporary case; in Girardian terms, the Inquisitor is the priest who manages the scapegoat mechanism. It also marks the limit of the right to believe: the problem is not belief, it is the Inquisitor.

In Nietzsche (*The Gay Science*, § 108, § 125 and § 343, 1882), not a thesis about the non-existence of God but an event in culture: belief in the Christian God has become unbelievable, and no one has yet measured everything that falls with it, beginning with morality. In § 125, the madman cries it out to the atheists of the marketplace, who laugh: we have killed him, you and I, and what festivals of atonement, what sacred games shall we have to invent? The Buddha's shadow remains for centuries in the cave (§ 108). The formula comes from Hegel, for whom the death of God in *Glauben und Wissen* (1802) is followed by a speculative resurrection; Nietzsche keeps the death without the resurrection. Heidegger makes it, in *The Word of Nietzsche: “God Is Dead”* (1943), the completion of metaphysics: Nietzsche completes, he does not leave. The essay retains that what triumphed over the Christian God is, according to *On the Genealogy of Morality* (III, 27), Christian morality itself, which announces Gauchet, and that the death of God is a task rather than an achievement. See also nihilism, Aufhebung.

Nietzsche's method (*Zur Genealogie der Moral*, 1887): to ask where our values come from and what will willed them, rather than whether they are true. Christian morality, the ressentiment of the weak, the priest's ascetic ideal are read in it as ways of evaluating that have a history and an interest. Religion appears as a value, not as an error or a symptom: this is the third regime of critique, distinct from those of Feuerbach and Marx, although Ricoeur groups them under the name of the school of suspicion. The third essay of the *Genealogy* (§ 24-28) applies the method to atheism itself: the will to truth is the last form of the ascetic ideal, which abolishes itself, and man would rather will nothingness than not will. William James answers all genealogies in advance: one knows the tree by its fruits, not by its roots. The essay calls genealogical lucidity the first common trait of the exceptions: knowing where one's fire comes from, like Nietzsche in § 344 of *The Gay Science*.

In Nietzsche, the devaluation of the highest values: when the true world collapses, nothing seems worth anything any more, and the question “what for?” remains unanswered. The word comes from Turgenev (*Fathers and Sons*, 1862) and the Russian debate; Dostoevsky stages it in *Demons* and in the formula, never proverbial in his work, that without God everything would be permitted. Nietzsche holds nihilism to be a consequence of Christian morality itself, which placed value in a beyond, then killed what guaranteed it; pity is for him the practice of nihilism (*The Antichrist* § 7), and the atheism of his contemporaries a nihilism unaware of itself. It is an ordeal to be passed through rather than a state in which to settle: *amor fati* is the way out of it. Camus, in *The Rebel* (1951), dates the beginning of the history of contemporary nihilism from Ivan's “everything is permitted” and reads in it the deification of history by the revolutionaries. The essay does not treat nihilism as an exit from religion but as what the refoundations claim to ward off. See also death of God, amor fati.

In Latin, love of fate. In Nietzsche (*The Gay Science* § 276, *Ecce Homo*), the consent that wills what is, wanting nothing else, neither forward nor backward nor in all eternity: not to bear necessity, but to love it. The essay distinguishes it from obedience to fate and from the justification of the world: to love necessity without justifying it is exactly what Ivan Karamazov refuses when he returns his ticket, and what Spinoza accomplishes through the intellectual love of God. It is an exercise that transforms the one who consents, not a submission to an absolute, which makes it a component of the spirituality of exercise. It has its limit: Nietzsche, an exception by attitude and not by position, remains unstable between § 344, which admits where his fire comes from, and Zarathustra's prophetic temptations. The essay's conclusion tries to hold together Spinoza's acceptance and Marx's protest, by consenting to the necessity of the world without consenting to the injustice of men. See also nihilism.

In Durkheim (*The Elementary Forms of Religious Life*, 1912), what is set apart and forbidden, as opposed to the profane; religion is a system of beliefs and practices relative to sacred things, which unites into one Church all those who adhere to them. The sacred is the form in which a society represents its own force to itself: the god is only the figurative expression of society, and the totem the hypostasized clan. It is born in collective effervescence, and the French Revolution, which made the Fatherland, Liberty and Reason sacred, is for Durkheim the proof of it. No society does without it: one does not leave the sacred, one exchanges one sacred for another, and the old gods grow old or die without others having been born. This is one of the two strongest objections to the essay's thesis, which answers it with Blumenberg and the sacrifice criterion. Otto gives its phenomenological version (the numinous), Girard the darkest version (the sacred is born of the murder of a victim), Bataille that of transgression, and Levinas rejects it as violence. See also numinous, scapegoat mechanism.

In Max Weber, the retreat of mysterious and incalculable powers before rational calculation: one can, in principle, master all things by foresight. The word, borrowed from Schiller, appears in *The Protestant Ethic* (1920 version) and in the lecture *Science as a Vocation* (1917, published 1919). The process is religious before it is scientific: Jewish prophecy, then ascetic Protestantism, drove magic out of the world, and religion abolished itself, just as in Nietzsche Christian morality killed the Christian God. Disenchantment does not mean the end of meaning but the impossibility of a guaranteed common meaning: the old gods, disenchanted, rise from their graves in the form of impersonal values at war, the polytheism of values; whoever cannot bear it may return to the arms of the old Churches, at the price of the sacrifice of the intellect. Gauchet takes up the formula in *The Disenchantment of the World* (1985) in a different sense, the exit from heteronomy. The essay sets Weber's gods returned in the plural against Durkheim's single Society and regards Weber as the last Puritan. See also secularization.

A word coined by Rudolf Otto from the Latin *numen*, divine power (*Das Heilige*, 1917), for the irrational element of the sacred, grasped by a feeling of its own that nothing else can replace: the terrible and fascinating mystery (*mysterium tremendum et fascinans*), the wholly other. The reader who has no experience of it is asked to read no further. Otto corrects Schleiermacher (attested response): the feeling of dependence is a creature-feeling, which presupposes the inaccessibility of its object, which would close Feuerbach's path; the essay declares itself not entirely convinced. He makes the sacred an a priori category of the mind, made up of rational and irrational moments: one cannot leave it, only leave it fallow or cultivate it, which makes it the paradoxical source of spiritualities without a Church. Jung defines religion by the scrupulous observation of the *numinosum*. Levinas answers that the numinous sacred is a violence from which Judaism has disenchanted the world. The essay describes the oceanic feeling as a numinous without *tremendum*, a pure *fascinans*. See also the sacred, oceanic feeling.

In Freud (*Die Zukunft einer Illusion*, 1927), in the technical sense: a belief commanded by a wish, which is not necessarily false, unlike error and delusion. Religion is an illusion because it repeats the infantile wish for a protecting father in the face of helplessness; it is the universal obsessional neurosis of humanity, and man creates the gods in the image of the father. This is the fifth regime of critique, which explains the need for the error where Feuerbach explained only the error: Freud sees man in miniature where Feuerbach saw man writ large (constructed confrontation). Freud sets against it “our god Logos”, science, which, he admits, is not very almighty; the essay reads in this its own thesis pronounced by the man who most resolutely wanted to refute it, and turns § 344 of *The Gay Science* against the sentence “our science is no illusion”. Romain Rolland answers him with the oceanic feeling. In the conclusion, Freud appears among the transfers of the sacred, for the god Logos. See also projection, oceanic feeling.

Romain Rolland's expression in his letter to Freud of 5 December 1927: a sensation of eternity, of being one with the world, without limits, which he held to be the true source of religion, independent of any dogma. Freud opens *Civilization and Its Discontents* (1930) with it: he admits that he cannot discover this feeling in himself, traces it back to the primary narcissism of the infant who does not yet distinguish himself from the world, suggests that it might aim at the restoration of an unlimited narcissism, and refuses to see in it the source of religion, which he finds in infantile helplessness and longing for the father (attested response). The essay judges that both are right: Freud about instituted religions, Rolland perhaps about experience, and describes the oceanic as a numinous without *tremendum*, a religion without a father but not without a mother. Comte-Sponville takes up the oceanic feeling in *L'Esprit de l'athéisme* (2006) and holds together Rolland's experience and Freud's atheism (constructed confrontation); the essay objects that the oceanic experience consoles and does not protest. See also illusion, numinous.

In Bergson (*The Two Sources of Morality and Religion*, 1932), the two religions humanity has produced. Static religion is born of the fabulating function, a defensive reaction of nature against what is depressing in intelligence, the representation of death and of the unforeseen; it is coextensive with our species, and Bergson describes it as a tissue of aberrations that protects society. Society is indeed a source, but the lowest one (attested response to Durkheim). Dynamic religion is that of the mystics, who cross in a leap the distance between the closed soul and the open soul, and whose impetus joins the creative impetus: God is love and the object of love, and he creates creators. Instituted religion is its cooled crystallization. Bergson thus answers, by constructed confrontation, Freud and Nietzsche: the overman exists, he is the mystic. The book ends on mysticism calling for mechanics and on the universe as a machine for making gods. The essay judges that Bergson escapes the deification of man by a narrow margin. See also the sacred, numinous.

A formula the tradition has drawn from *Freud and Philosophy: An Essay on Interpretation* (1965), where Ricoeur places Marx, Nietzsche and Freud in a single school of suspicion: all three read consciousness as a text to be deciphered, whose apparent meaning conceals a hidden meaning, class interest, will to power, desire, and invent a mediate science of meaning. Ricoeur sets against them a hermeneutics of restoration, that of Eliade and of the phenomenology of religion, and proposes a faith that has passed through criticism, the second naïveté, among men who have not finished putting idols to death and are only beginning to hear symbols. The god of accusation, whom Nietzsche destroys, and the god of consolation, whom Freud destroys, are rightly destroyed. The essay finds him right about method and wrong about the object: the three regimes, symptom, genealogy, illusion, remain distinct and do not form a school. In the conclusion, Ricoeur appears among the believing exceptions, cautious and unstable. See also second naïveté, genealogy.

In Ricoeur (*The Symbolism of Evil*, 1960; the formula circulates in French retranslated from English), the way of believing that returns to symbols after passing through criticism: no longer the immediate adherence of the first believer, lost beyond recovery, but a listening schooled by suspicion, in which the symbol gives rise to thought. It presupposes that interpretation has no end and that faith never becomes knowledge again. The essay addresses to it the objection of Hegel and of Leo Strauss: a second naïveté might be only a first one that gives itself a good conscience; it retains the answer of Ricoeur, for whom it is not a knowledge but a listening, and reconstructs from him a belief without a father that would escape Freud's suspicion. Ricoeur also hears, in religion, Marx's Protest. With Jaspers and Weil, he is a believing exception: he refounds nothing, but his position remains unstable. See also masters of suspicion.

In Edward Tylor (*Primitive Culture*, 1871), belief in spiritual beings, which he takes to be the minimal definition of religion. Animism is a primitive philosophy: the man of the earliest ages, reasoning about dreams, visions and death, concludes that there exists a soul separable from the body, then peoples the world with spirits; survivals of this stage persist in the higher religions, and anthropology presents itself as a reformer's science. Frazer extends the scheme in *The Golden Bough* through the succession of magic (the bastard sister of science), religion and science. The essay sees in it the regime of error in its evolutionist form: Tylor and Frazer explain the birth of belief, not its duration. Durkheim objects that a universal and everyday error would be an inexplicable delusion; Wittgenstein, in his remarks on Frazer, that the rite expresses and does not reason, and that Frazer is more savage than his savages (attested response); Malinowski, that magic begins where knowledge stops. Girard takes up all of Frazer's material while reversing its interpretation. What remains established: the universality of belief in invisible beings.

In René Girard (*Violence and the Sacred*, 1972), the origin of the sacred. A community ravaged by mimetic crisis, in which each imitates the other's violence and differences are effaced, suddenly recovers its unity by discharging its violence onto a single victim, designated by some arbitrary trait; the returning peace is attributed to the victim itself, which becomes sacred, at once guilty and beneficent, accursed and divine. Myth is the account of the lynching from the point of view of the lynchers; rite is its controlled repetition on a substitute victim, sacrifice; prohibitions prevent the return of the crisis. The mechanism requires misrecognition: lynchers who knew their victim to be innocent would not obtain peace. For Girard, the Bible and the Gospels, which tell the Passion from the point of view of the innocent victim, unveil the mechanism and render it inoperative. The essay keeps the anthropological level, which gives the sacrifice criterion its foundation (to refound is to designate a victim, and the Grand Inquisitor is the priest of the mechanism), and leaves aside the apologetic level: the exit from sacrifice belongs to anyone who refuses the crowd, believer or not. See also mimetic desire, the sacred.

In Girard (*Deceit, Desire, and the Novel*, 1961), desire that imitates the desire of another: one does not desire an object directly, one desires it because a model desires it. Don Quixote wants to be a knight because Amadis was one; Emma Bovary loves through the novels she has read. Desire is not a straight line between a subject and an object, but a triangle whose apex is a mediator. When the model is distant, imitation is harmless; when he is close and desires the same object in the same world, he becomes a rival, the rival an obstacle, and the obstacle an even more fascinating model. Rivalry spreads by imitation up to the mimetic crisis, the war of all against all, which the scapegoat mechanism resolves. Girard reproaches Freud with having tied the founding murder to sexual desire and the father rather than to mimetic rivalry and the arbitrary victim (attested response). The essay retains mimetic desire as the anthropological hypothesis that grounds its criterion, and distinguishes this hypothesis from the Christian apologetics added to it. See also scapegoat mechanism.

Rudolf Bultmann's programme (lecture *Neues Testament und Mythologie*, 1941): to interpret existentially the message of the New Testament, the kerygma, by freeing it from the mythical world picture that envelops it, the three storeys of the universe, miracles, demons, the end of time, which has become unbelievable for modern man. The aim is not to eliminate myth, as in Strauss, but to translate it into the language of existence, borrowed from Heidegger: faith is a decision before God's call, not an opinion about facts. Bultmann thus separates the Christ of the kerygma, object of faith, from the Jesus of history, about whom almost nothing can be known. Jaspers objects to him in 1953, in *Die Frage der Entmythologisierung* (1954), that myth cannot be translated without loss and is the proper language of transcendence (attested response); Bonhoeffer judges Bultmann a liberal at bottom. The essay meets it in the debate on Jesus' existence and in Part Ten. See also kerygma, mythicist thesis.

From the Greek *kêrugma*, the herald's proclamation: the proclamation of the earliest Christian faith, that Christ died for our sins, was buried and was raised on the third day, of which Paul transmits the oldest formula (1 Co 15, 3-5), received from before him. Twentieth-century exegesis, Bultmann above all, uses the word to distinguish the Christ of the kerygma, object of faith and preaching, from the Jesus of history, object of historical inquiry: the Gospels are testimonies of faith, not biographies. In the debate on Jesus' existence, the essay holds that what matters is not knowing whether Jesus lived, which the consensus of historians affirms, but how a crucified prophet became the incarnate Logos; the kerygma is the first moment of this transformation, which Paul completes by spiritualizing sacrifice (Rm 12, 1) instead of abolishing it. See also demythologization, Logos.

The thesis that Jesus did not exist and is a mythical construction: sketched by Bruno Bauer, developed by Arthur Drews (*Die Christusmythe*, 1909) and Paul-Louis Couchoud (1924, answered by Goguel in 1925), taken up by Richard Carrier (2014) and popularized by Onfray (*Théorie de Jésus*, 2023). It is marginal: the historical existence of Jesus is the consensus of historians, believers, agnostics and atheists alike, based on Paul (Ga 1, 19 ; 4, 4 ; 1 Co 15), the criteria of embarrassment in the Gospels, Josephus and Tacitus; Celsus, Nietzsche and Engels did not doubt it. The essay devotes a section of Part Two to it and places it in the regime of error, in its naive form; it notes that Drews denies Jesus in order to found a monist religion, a textbook case of the law of refoundations, and that the question matters little: what counts is the transformation of a crucified prophet into the incarnate Logos. See also kerygma, demythologization.

Georges Bataille's project, which gathers *Inner Experience* (1943), *Guilty* (1944) and *On Nietzsche* (1945) under the title *Somme athéologique*: the title parodies the *Summa Theologiae* of Thomas Aquinas and announces an undertaking of the same scope, but of opposite meaning. Atheology is an inner experience of the sacred without God, a journey to the end of the possible of man, a naked experience that leads thought to non-knowledge, through anguish, laughter, ecstasy and expenditure. Sartre sees in him a new mystic of whom only the corpse can still be touched (attested response, 1943). Michel Onfray takes up the word in 2005 in his *Traité d'athéologie*, in an entirely different sense, that of a militant critique of the three monotheisms, which the essay calls a reversal. It regards Bataille as a key witness, not as an exception: his sacred of transgression refounds a sacred and confirms Durkheim. See also the sacred.

In Jean-Luc Marion (*The Idol and Distance*, 1977; *God Without Being*, 1982), two ways of aiming at the divine. The idol stops the gaze and sends back to it its own measure: an invisible mirror, it is on the scale of the one who looks at it. The icon lets the gaze pass through it towards what exceeds it, and looks back at it in return. There are conceptual idols: the god of onto-theology, with its site, metaphysics, its function, theology within onto-theo-logy, and its definition, the *causa sui*, is one; Heidegger, who subjects God to the question of being, provides for Marion a second, and God is not said first of all on the basis of Being. Marion thus turns the Zurich seminar against Heidegger (attested response), and in 1995 qualified his judgement on Thomas Aquinas. The essay draws from it its assessment of twentieth-century Christianity: at once a victory and a capitulation, a purified faith that has renounced knowing, consoling, founding and instituting, and of which there remains a spirituality that atheists also claim. See also onto-theology.
